syllabus.clause: the analysis, redo and undo passes, compensation log records and fuzzy checkpoints. Why steal + no-force is the high-performance buffer policy, and when a simpler redo-only design (no-steal, typical of LSM engines) is enough.

The same paper names the buffer policy this topic's own recovery assumes: steal, allowing an uncommitted page to be written back early, and no-force, allowing a committed one to stay unwritten. Redo and undo together are exactly why that combination is safe

items.item: The redo-reapplies-everyone claim deliberately runs redo alone, before undo, against a log with one committed and one never-committed transaction's updates, so the measurement is specifically that redo itself carries no notion of commit status, not merely that the final recovered state happens to be correct.

at.step: Measured: redo genuinely reapplied the uncommitted transaction's own updates too, exactly like the committed one's; nothing about redo itself tells them apart

items.item: The checkpoint-bound measurement seeds the bounded redo's own starting pages with the value actually already on disk at checkpoint time, not with blanks, matching what a real recovery's own redo pass starts from; the full-scan comparison instead starts from blanks to show what redo would need to reconstruct without that known state.

at.step: Measured: redo starting from the checkpoint's own bound visited genuinely fewer log records, and reached the exact same final state as a full scan from the start

items.item: The record count comparison between the full scan and the checkpoint-bounded scan counts only Update and CLR records actually applied to a page, not every record type, since a checkpoint or commit record carries no page content for redo to apply in the first place.

at.step: Measured: redo starting from the checkpoint's own bound visited genuinely fewer log records, and reached the exact same final state as a full scan from the start

items.item: The bounded-undo measurement deliberately interrupts undo after exactly one of the loser transaction's two updates, then discards the in-memory page state entirely and reruns the complete analysis, redo, and undo sequence from scratch, so the claim is about a genuine second, independent recovery attempt, not a single continuous run that merely paused.

at.step: Measured: the second recovery resumed undo exactly where the first one left off; the already-undone update got exactly one compensation log record, total, across both attempts

items.item: Analysis determines each loser's own undo-resumption point from the most recent record belonging to that transaction, whether that record is a plain update or a CLR already written on an earlier attempt; the undo pass itself then follows a CLR's own undo_next_lsn pointer forward rather than ever re-examining the record the CLR already compensated for.

at.step: Measured: the second recovery resumed undo exactly where the first one left off; the already-undone update got exactly one compensation log record, total, across both attempts

items.item: The syllabus names a simpler, redo-only, no-steal design, typical of LSM engines, as sufficient when immutable, append-only writes mean an uncommitted page is never written back before commit in the first place; this topic discusses that alternative in prose rather than building a second recovery implementation, since the claim under test is specifically why steal and no-force need both an undo pass and CLRs, not a full comparison implementation.
